words.problem: Multi-tenant apps usually trust every query to filter by tenant. One forgotten filter leaks another customer's tickets. I wanted a platform where a cross-tenant read is not a bug you can write.

approach.title: Five layers of isolation
approach.body: Composite (orgId, id) foreign keys make a cross-tenant reference unrepresentable. The tenant comes from the credential, never the host. Every repository method takes an explicit orgId. approach.title: Four ITIL records, four lifecycles
approach.body: Incidents, service requests, problems and changes are modeled as different things with their own states. Priority is computed from impact and urgency, never typed into a dropdown.

approach.title: Invariants you can run
approach.body: A db:doctor script asserts the isolation guarantees actually hold against a live database, so the architecture is tested, not just described.

patchgrid.subject: Update the Patchgrid case study through milestone 12

words.tagline: Multi-tenant IT service management with isolation enforced by the database.
words.summary: Patchgrid is a ticketing and operations platform for IT and security teams. Each company gets its own subdomain, and its data is isolated at the database level through five independent layers, not by remembering a WHERE clause. Twelve milestones in, it covers incidents, requests, problems and changes, SLA clocks, email intake, a knowledge base, assets, an operator back-office that never impersonates, signed webhooks and reports that answer in under 25 ms at 100,000 tickets.
words.problem: Multi-tenant apps usually trust every query to filter by tenant. One forgotten filter leaks another customer's tickets. I wanted a platform where a cross-tenant read is not a bug you can write.

approach.title: Five layers of isolation
approach.body: Composite (orgId, id) foreign keys make a cross-tenant reference unrepresentable, because Postgres checks foreign keys with row security off. The tenant comes from the credential, never the host. Every repository method takes an explicit orgId. A Prisma client extension sets a transaction-local config and throws without context. Postgres enforces it all with forced row level security and an app role that cannot bypass it.

approach.title: Four ITIL records, four lifecycles
approach.body: Incidents, service requests, problems and changes are modeled as different things with their own states and one transition endpoint. Priority is computed from impact and urgency, and a client that sends one gets a 400. SLA clocks run around the clock, pause while waiting on the requester, and are swept per tenant.

approach.title: Everything a desk needs
approach.body: Mail to the workspace becomes a ticket if it passes DMARC, and replies thread onto it. A versioned knowledge base suggests articles while a requester types. Assets link to tickets. Uploads go straight to object storage on a separate domain and are checked by their bytes, not their names.

approach.title: A platform layer that cannot peek
approach.body: Operators work at admin. with their own login and second factor, see metadata and never content, and read a workspace only in an owner-granted, read-only, time-boxed support session written to that workspace's audit log. API tokens are service accounts whose scopes intersect a role. Deleting a workspace leaves a nameless tombstone after 30 days.

approach.title: Delivery you can replay
approach.body: A transactional outbox is read per tenant in transaction-id order below the snapshot horizon, so nothing is lost, repeated or skipped. Notifications, signed webhooks with retries and a circuit breaker, and reporting are its consumers. Reports come from their own read model so they never compete with the queues.

approach.title: Invariants you can run
approach.body: A tenancy suite asserts 13 catalog and 37 isolation invariants against a live database on every merge, a doctor script checks the roles and privileges, and every integration fixture creates two organizations so a leak fails a test. A Playwright suite drives two tenants through the browser, with negative cases.

approach.title: Reviewed before shipping
approach.body: A threat model with eleven trust boundaries, three independent read-only security reviews at milestone 9 that found 16 issues, all fixed in the same change set, and further reviews at each milestone since. Traces and metrics are labelled by tenant, so a Grafana board answers which tenant is slow.

highlights: Subdomain per tenant across one monorepo: marketing, workspace, operator back-office and API
Row level security forced on every tenant table, composite keys across tenants
Priority derived from impact x urgency, four lifecycles behind one transition endpoint
Email intake gated by DMARC, knowledge base, assets, presigned uploads
No impersonation, ever: support sessions are granted, read-only, audited and time-boxed
Transactional outbox, Standard Webhooks, reports under 25 ms at 100,000 tickets
Member MFA with step-up, OpenTelemetry per tenant, CodeQL on every change

words.problem: JWT bugs hide in the details: alg=none, algorithm confusion, weak HMAC secrets, keys smuggled in the header. Most libraries hide those details on purpose.

approach.title: Audit without a key
approach.body: Static checks flag alg=none, weak HMAC, jwk in the header and other CVE-referenced misconfigurations before you even have the secret.

approach.title: Attack your own verifier
approach.body: Forge attack-shaped variants such as alg=none and algorithm confusion, then point them at your own service to prove it rejects them.

approach.title: Honest cryptography
approach.body: Constant-time signature comparison, JWKS verification of standard claims, a streamed multi-threaded wordlist cracker and strong secret generation.

highlights: Published on PyPI, installable with pipx or uv
Decode, audit, verify, sign, forge, crack, generate
JSON output for scripting

jwt-toolkit.subject: Update JWT Toolkit case study for v1.1.0

words.tagline: Inspect, compare and stress-test JWTs, with verification you can read.
words.summary: A Python security CLI for debugging token changes, checking signatures and testing your own verifier. Version 1.1.0 adds token diffs, EdDSA and practical key inputs while tightening parsing, claim validation and scriptable errors. The JWS logic stays readable on top of cryptography, without pyjwt or python-jose.
words.problem: A decoded token can look convincing while its verifier accepts an invalid expiry, ignores a critical header or trusts the wrong algorithm. Debugging those failures also means comparing claims, handling real keys and getting dependable results into CI.

approach.title: Make verification boundaries explicit
approach.body: Verification matches algorithm names case-sensitively, rejects unsupported crit headers and non-finite or non-numeric time claims, and expires a token at its exp second. Headers and payloads must be JSON objects. These fixes close acceptance edge cases and turn malformed input into a reported error instead of a crash.

approach.title: Explain what changed between tokens
approach.body: The new diff command walks nested headers and payloads with JSON Pointer paths, highlighting identity, permission and lifetime fields. It preserves array order and JSON types, and distinguishes encoding-only changes from changed claims. JSON output and an optional failure exit code make it useful for regression checks; comparison does not verify either token.

approach.title: Work with the keys applications use
approach.body: Ed25519, Ed448 and EdDSA join HMAC, RSA, RSA-PSS and ECDSA, including OKP keys from JWKS. X.509 certificates and encrypted private keys reduce key-conversion work. Secret files keep HMAC values out of command arguments, while payload files, relative lifetimes and raw secret output make test fixtures easier to script.

approach.title: Crack the candidates you actually supplied
approach.body: Wordlist lines retain spaces, leading # characters and non-UTF-8 bytes, so valid candidates are no longer silently changed or skipped. Bounded batches run in worker processes to bypass CPython's GIL, preserving the first match in wordlist order. Small lists avoid process startup costs, and a bundled list makes the command usable immediately after installation.

approach.title: Keep security findings honest
approach.body: Keyless audits flag risky headers, missing claims and weak configurations; --require now checks every named claim, including custom ones. Forge produces attack-shaped tokens for your own verifier and labels header-only variants whose rejection cannot rule out the named flaw. Untrusted text renders literally, preventing crafted claims from crashing or restyling terminal reports.

approach.title: Ship a CLI that automation can trust
approach.body: Every --json failure path returns an error document with a stable code. Wordlist downloads stay on verified TLS and use the installed release's tag. Before PyPI publication, the tagged commit must pass tests, coverage, lint, types and security checks, and its tag must match the package version. Trusted Publishing adds distribution attestations.

highlights: v1.1.0 released on 17 October 2026, installable with pipx or uv
Token diffs with JSON Pointer paths and CI exit codes
EdDSA, JWKS, certificates and encrypted private keys
UTC and relative timestamps for decoded time claims
Bundled wordlist and bounded process-based cracking
Stable JSON errors and a validated PyPI publishing workflow

words.tagline: Keeps a Mac awake exactly as long as the work is alive, then lets it sleep.
words.summary: A session-aware wake controller for macOS: a menu bar app, a CLI and a local control endpoint over a Unix socket. A running process, a listening port, a wrapped command, a coding agent's session, a chosen app or a timer each hold the machine open, and the hold releases itself when the last one ends. When it does, the Mac can notify you, sleep or shut down.
words.problem: Keep-awake tools are a switch you flip on and forget to flip off. They model a timer, not the thing you actually care about: the build, the dev server, the agent that will finish at some point in the night.

approach.title: Sessions, not switches
approach.body: Tell it what to watch: a build, a dev server on :3000, a process id, an app, a Claude Code or Codex session, or just twenty minutes. Every session is one type conforming to one protocol, and the Mac is awake exactly while at least one is active. Nothing toggles the power assertion directly; one reconcile step derives it from the sessions.

approach.title: Leases, not goodbyes
approach.body: Agent hooks open a lease keyed by the session id and renew it on every event. A crash or a kill never sends an end hook, so the lease's expiry is the source of truth, not the goodbye. The hooks are no-ops when the app is not running, so they never block the agent.

approach.title: Cleans up after itself
approach.body: When the last session ends it can notify, sleep the display, sleep the Mac, shut down or restart. Each action is armed per occasion, shown in the menu and cancelable. Run the agent overnight, shut down when it finishes.

approach.title: Guardrails for the battery
approach.body: A hold can release itself on battery, below a chosen charge or in Low Power Mode. The display stays on by default, with one switch to let it sleep while the system stays awake. The system-level assertion that fights the lid is never used.

approach.title: Legible
approach.body: The menu lists every reason the Mac is awake, including other apps' power assertions like a call, audio or a stray caffeinate, named by their owning process. Wakehold's own holds show up in pmset like everyone else's.

approach.title: A socket, not a port
approach.body: The CLI and hooks talk to the app over HTTP on a Unix domain socket under Application Support, mode 0600 with a peer check. A localhost port would be reachable from a browser and any local process; a socket is scoped by the filesystem, and curl still works.

highlights: Menu bar app, CLI and a control endpoint over a Unix socket
Watches processes, ports, commands, agents, apps and timers
Hooks for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor with crash-safe leases
Post-session sleep, shutdown, restart or notify; battery guardrails
Localised in English and Arabic, with mirrored layout
Native Swift with IOKit power assertions, no Electron

dir-analysis-tool.subject: Update the dir-analysis-tool case study for v3.0.0

words.tagline: Find out what is taking up space: largest folders, duplicates, stale files and size budgets for CI, in one pass.
words.summary: dat is a memory-bounded directory analyzer for the terminal and for CI. It walks a tree once and reports the largest folders and files, duplicated content, empty and stale files and a breakdown by type, then prints it as a table, JSON, Markdown, CSV or a single-file HTML report. Version 3 adds directory diffs, a watch mode, size budgets that fail a build, and a typed library API that returns exactly what the CLI prints.
words.problem: Disk audits either load everything into memory or give you a wall of output you cannot act on or pipe anywhere. The ones that are fast tend to lie a little: they count hard links twice, follow symlink cycles, or skip unreadable paths without saying so.

approach.title: One walk, bounded memory
approach.body: Every file is stat'ed exactly once. Top-N lists live in bounded heaps, one concurrency limiter covers every filesystem call so wide trees cannot exhaust handles, and depth-first scheduling keeps the queue small. The author's benchmark holds about 9 MB for 140,000 files.

approach.title: Duplicates in three stages
approach.body: Files are grouped by size first. Candidates over 256 KiB are then compared by a SHA-256 sample of their first and last 64 KiB, and only survivors get a full streaming hash with reused buffers. Most files are never read in full, which made duplicates about four times faster than version 2.

approach.title: Answers that point somewhere
approach.body: The headline is the largest folders, and a folder that is 95% one child folds into it so the list points at where the data lives instead of repeating parents. Large, stale, empty and duplicate files come with totals you can act on, and ordering is by size then path, never discovery order.

approach.title: Budgets, diffs and a watch
approach.body: Rules like size<=2MB or duplicates=0 fail a build with exit code 2 and name the rule. dat compare lists what was added, removed and changed between two trees, by content on request. dat watch follows a folder with native filesystem events and streams NDJSON.

approach.title: Five outputs, one shape
approach.body: Pretty, JSON with a versioned schema, Markdown for a pull request summary, CSV with a section column and neutralised formula cells, and an HTML report in a single file with inline charts and a content security policy that blocks all network access. Progress and warnings go to stderr; stdout carries only the report.

approach.title: A library that is the CLI
approach.body: analyze, compare and every renderer are exported as typed ESM, and the library's return value is exactly what --format json prints. Releases are cut by semantic-release from conventional commits with npm provenance, after a matrix of three operating systems and three Node versions passes.

highlights: Largest folders, largest files, duplicates, stale and empty files, type breakdown
Size budgets for CI that exit 2, directory diffs and a watch mode
Pretty, JSON, Markdown, CSV and single-file HTML output
Hard links counted once, symlink cycles detected, unreadable paths reported
Typed library API with the same results as the CLI
Published with npm provenance after tests on macOS, Linux and Windows

words.problem: Ruler tools live inside one browser tab or one design app, so you cannot line up a native window against a design mockup, or measure the gap between two things that belong to different programs.

approach.title: Real pixels
approach.body: Tick labels respect each screen's backing scale factor, so 100 means 100 actual display pixels on any screen. Guides are stored in physical pixels per display, and a small core library owns every point-to-pixel conversion so the arithmetic is unit tested without a screen.

approach.title: Out of the way
approach.body: Transparent, non-activating panels sit over each display. They ignore mouse events except on the two ruler strips while guide placement is on, and while measure, crosshair, sampler or loupe owns the pointer. Everything else clicks through.

approach.title: Measure, then take it with you
approach.body: Drag a box for width by height, or Option-drag two points for distance and angle. Measurements stay held on screen, click one to remove it, and the size copies in any of five formats including CSS, with optional position and aspect-ratio badges.

approach.title: Read the screen itself
approach.body: The color sampler reads the pixel under the pointer as hex and RGB through ScreenCaptureKit, excluding Gauge's own windows from the capture. The loupe magnifies the same feed with a pixel grid, the exact coordinate and its color.

approach.title: Guides that stay put

words.tagline: Every running process and open port on your Mac, one click from the menu bar.
words.summary: A menu bar app that lists processes and open network ports side by side, refreshed every few seconds, filtered as you type, and lets you end either by PID: gracefully by default and forcefully one right-click away. It always tells you why something would not die.
words.problem: Killing a stray dev server means kill -9 $(lsof -ti:3000) or three windows of Activity Monitor, and neither tells you why a process survived.

approach.title: Two lists, one action
approach.body: Processes with CPU, memory and user, and ports with their process, protocol and bind address, share one control. SIGTERM by default; SIGKILL is a separate affordance behind a right-click or a hover, never the default button, so a slip of the mouse cannot force-kill anything.

approach.title: Never fails silently
approach.body: Every attempt reports what happened: severed, denied because the process is root-owned or protected, already gone, or a readable error. Already gone is treated as success, since the goal was for it to stop.

approach.title: Fresh enough, and pausable
approach.body: Both lists poll every three seconds off the main thread, pause on request, refresh on demand and stop when the panel closes. One search field matches name, PID, address, port or protocol, and processes sort by CPU, memory, name or PID.

approach.title: Honest about its sources
approach.body: Today the lists come from ps and lsof, parsed by pure functions that are tested against captured output. Both listers sit behind protocols so a libproc implementation can drop in later without touching the interface. Killing calls kill(2) directly.

highlights: No Dock icon, no permissions requested, no App Sandbox
Live refresh every three seconds, search as you type, sortable
SIGTERM by default, SIGKILL one right-click away
Honest error reporting, including processes it is not allowed to kill
Monospaced, dense and scannable

words.tagline: Break reminders delivered by a small desktop character that knows when to stay quiet.
words.summary: Instead of a notification you swipe away on reflex, a character slides in from a screen corner, says one short thing, and leaves. It holds reminders during calls, full screen video, a locked screen or a calendar event and delivers them one at a time once the moment clears. Reminders are typed in plain words: water every 45 minutes, stretch at 3pm on weekdays.
words.problem: Break reminders are banners you dismiss without reading, and they interrupt at the worst moments. The apps that solve this with a character are paid and closed.

approach.title: Never at a bad moment
approach.body: No reminders while the camera or microphone is in use, a window is full screen, the screen is locked or you are away, and optionally while a calendar event is on. Held reminders queue in order and drain one at a time; the queue is never flushed, because nobody wants four characters in a row after a meeting.

approach.title: The moment after
approach.body: When a long call or full-screen stretch ends, a reminder that was nearly due arrives right then. Coming back from a real break restarts every interval, so you are not told to move five minutes after you did.

approach.title: Reminders in plain words
approach.body: Press a global shortcut anywhere and type water every 45 minutes, call Tom at 3 or stretch at 3pm on weekdays. A deterministic on-device parser turns it into a repeating, one-time or weekday reminder with its own mood. Presets retune the four built-ins in one click.

approach.title: Never guilts you
approach.body: No streaks, no sad faces. Ignore it and it leaves on its own after a few seconds. Quiet hours, per-reminder active hours, snooze and a minimum gap between appearances keep it from nagging.

approach.title: Three layers, one seam
approach.body: The scheduler decides when and never touches AppKit, the presenter decides how it looks and never decides timing, and reminders are plain data in a documented JSON file you can hand-edit. The character, the app icon and the menu bar mark are drawn from the same geometry in code.

highlights: Free and open source, unlike every comparable app with a character
Plain-words quick add with a global shortcut, no AI and no network
Holds for calls, full screen, lock, idle and optional calendar events
One-time, weekday and repeating reminders, presets and quiet hours
Native Swift, menu bar only, hand-editable reminders.json

drainscope.subject: Add drainscope, the Linux energy monitor

words.tagline: Per-app battery and energy usage for the Linux desktop, measured from hardware counters.
words.summary: drainscope measures energy from RAPL counters and the battery, attributes it to apps, terminal workloads and system services, keeps local history, and shows it on the command line, in GNOME's quick settings and in a desktop app. No component runs as root.
words.problem: Windows, macOS and Android have told you which app drained the battery for years. Linux hasn't. The counters exist, but they are root-only, they measure the whole machine, and nothing attributes them to the apps that spent the energy.

approach.title: Measure, then attribute
approach.body: Every 5 seconds a user service reads RAPL energy counters, the batteries, cgroup v2 CPU time and GPU time from DRM fdinfo. Energy above the machine's learned idle floor goes to whoever was active, reconciled against the battery over 10 second windows, so apps, terminal workloads and systemd services each get their share.

approach.title: Least privilege, by construction
approach.body: No component runs as root. A sandboxed sampler with a single capability reads the root-only counters and serves them over D-Bus only to the active local session, rate-limited and quantized against the Platypus side channel. An optional eBPF probe counts CPU wakeups and per-app network bytes without ever seeing addresses or contents. Both are confined by SELinux and exit when idle.

approach.title: Where you already look
approach.body: History stays on your machine. A CLI answers the questions people actually ask (since unplugged, the last 24 hours, live power, battery lost in suspend, what keeps waking the CPU, battery wear), a GNOME Shell quick settings menu shows the same numbers, and a desktop app draws them on a stacked timeline.

highlights: No component runs as root; sampler and probe each hold only the capabilities they need
Signed RPMs for Fedora 44, 45 and rawhide on COPR
Validated against real hardware, with recorded traces replayed in tests
Nothing leaves the machine; no component uses the network

On the development laptop, idle CPU use on battery fell from 0.82–1.0% to 0.28% of one CPU.

drainscope.subject: Update DrainScope case study for v1.0.0

words.tagline: See where your Linux laptop's battery goes, by app, terminal command and service.
words.summary: drainscope measures energy from hardware counters and the battery, then estimates each app's share, including time in use and in the background. A GNOME Quick Settings extension, desktop app and CLI show local history, sleep loss, battery health, wakeups and network activity. Version 1.0.0 is the first stable release, backed by failure testing and a 48-hour soak test on the development laptop.
words.problem: A battery percentage says how much charge is left, but not which app spent it or whether it was working in the background. Linux exposes energy and activity counters across the kernel and desktop, with different permissions and gaps in hardware support. I wanted to turn those readings into a useful account of where the battery went, without running a monitor as root.

approach.title: Measure the total, explain each share
approach.body: RAPL counters and battery readings provide the measured energy. A user service combines cgroup v2 CPU time and GPU time from DRM fdinfo to estimate each consumer's share above a learned idle floor. Model v4 also shares energy by CPU time when RAPL is unavailable. Network softirq and threaded interrupt work follow the apps' measured traffic, while Idle and Display & devices remain visible parts of the total.

approach.title: In use or in the background
approach.body: The GNOME extension reports the focused app's ID, never its window title. The daemon uses focused time to split each app's energy into in use, background and unknown, shown in app details, CLI reports and exports. Without focus data, the split stays unknown; terminal tabs and services are not classified. In a controlled test with two equal loads, in-use energy shares matched focused-time shares within 0.6 percentage points.

approach.title: Three ways into the same history
approach.body: GNOME 50 and 51 get a Quick Settings tile showing the top consumers since unplugging. The GTK and libadwaita app adds a stacked timeline, per-consumer detail and views for the last hour, 24 hours or 7 days. The CLI adds live power and reports filtered by period, consumer kind or power source. Lists stay stable as readings change, and the app follows daemon stops and restarts with clear status messages.

approach.title: Activity, sleep and battery wear
approach.body: The optional eBPF probe counts per-app CPU wakeups and network bytes, excluding loopback traffic. Sleep history records battery loss and reports wake reasons only when reliable. Daily battery-health records track capacity against design and charge cycles. Attribution pauses across suspend, and the since-unplugged session resets after charging while the machine was off.

approach.title: Least privilege and local history
approach.body: No component runs as root or opens a network socket. The sampler and optional probe run as dedicated users with one and three Linux capabilities respectively, confined by systemd sandboxes and SELinux where enabled. polkit restricts counter access to the active local session; readings are rate-limited and coarsened. Energy and focus history stay in the user's local SQLite database.

approach.title: Keep measuring when parts fail
approach.body: The daemon can start without writable history, using in-memory storage, and keeps measuring when the disk fills. Missing sampler or probe services degrade the available readings instead of stopping collection. It recovers from an unreadable database, stops safely on a newer schema, and handles counter resets after service restarts. A documented failure checklist covers denied permissions, missing services, full disks and desktop restarts; drainscope doctor explains what needs attention.

approach.title: A stable release with measured overhead
approach.body: Sampling slows to every 15 seconds when no view is watching and returns to 5 seconds while a view is open. Batched readings, faster history queries and a once-a-minute refresh for the 7-day view keep the cost down. Across a 48-hour soak of the code shipped as 1.0, the daemon averaged 0.179% of one CPU and peaked at 14.1 MB on the development laptop, with no service warnings, extension errors or SELinux denials. These are daemon figures, not the cost of all components combined.

approach.title: Reports you can take with you
approach.body: Summary, report, sleep, health, wakeups and network views export every row as CSV or JSON in joules, watts and Unix seconds. Reports include foreground, background and unknown energy plus focused time; JSON includes the period, measured coverage and model version. Unknown readings stay distinct from zero, including history recorded before focus tracking existed.

approach.title: Packaged, documented and upgradeable
approach.body: The first stable release ships signed COPR packages for Fedora 44, 45 and rawhide, with installation checked on Fedora 44 and 45. Updates arrive through dnf and restart the daemon. Release downloads also include Fedora 44 RPMs and the extension zip. Architecture, installation, troubleshooting and contribution guides accompany the release; the extensions.gnome.org listing is still awaiting review.

approach.title: Make the limits visible
approach.body: Validation uses recorded trace replays and real measurements on an Intel i7-8550U laptop with i915 graphics. AMD Zen support is expected from fixtures but has not been tested on real hardware; its integrated-GPU energy is split by CPU time, and Intel xe GPU energy is not yet split per app. Light, bursty work remains undercharged by proportional sharing. The published model and validation explain these limits rather than presenting per-app estimates as direct measurements.

highlights: First stable release, v1.0.0, published on October 14, 2026
Foreground and background energy in app details, CLI reports and exports, with unknown time kept explicit
Model v4 supports battery-only attribution alongside CPU, GPU and network activity accounting
Per-app wakeups and traffic, suspend loss and daily battery-health history
48-hour soak test with 0.18% average daemon CPU and 14.1 MB peak daemon memory on the development laptop
Failure recovery checked across missing services, permission denials, full disks and restarts
Signed Fedora 44, 45 and rawhide packages; GNOME 50 and 51 support
Local history, no network access and no component running as root

words.tagline: A complete authentication backend: email verification, two-factor sign-in, refresh tokens and rate limits, ready to fork.
words.summary: An Express and TypeScript authentication service on PostgreSQL and Prisma. It covers sign-up with an emailed one-time code, password reset, TOTP two-factor authentication with QR enrolment, short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, and a login history, with rate limiting and input sanitization on every endpoint.
words.problem: Every project needs authentication, and rushed implementations skip the same parts: verifying the email, a second factor, token rotation and rate limits. This template ships them already done.

approach.title: The whole account lifecycle
approach.body: Sign-up sends a one-time code by email through the Gmail API, with resend, forgot and reset password flows, and a login history per user.

approach.title: Two factors, two tokens
approach.body: TOTP two-factor authentication with QR code enrolment, verification, sign-in and disable flows. Sessions use 20 minute access tokens and 7 day refresh tokens.

approach.title: Hostile input assumed
approach.body: Rate limits on every authentication endpoint, Zod validation, HTML sanitization, strong password rules that reject common passwords, bcrypt with configurable rounds, security headers and CORS.

highlights: TOTP two-factor authentication with QR enrolment
Email verification and password reset by one-time code
Rate limiting on every authentication endpoint
Short-lived access tokens, longer-lived refresh tokens

node-authentication-template.subject: Refresh auth, drainscope and Repo Scout portfolio content

words.tagline: Passkeys, OpenID Connect and revocable sessions in an authentication backend ready to fork.
words.summary: An Express 5 and TypeScript authentication API on PostgreSQL and Prisma 7, with passwordless passkeys, TOTP recovery codes and a headless OpenID Connect provider. Rotating tokens, account self-service, reliable email delivery and tracing cover the work around sign-in too.
words.problem: Authentication is more than issuing a token. People need passwordless sign-in, a way to recover a second factor, control over their sessions and their data, and an identity other apps can trust. The starter should handle those lifecycles together.

approach.title: Passkeys and a recoverable second factor
approach.body: WebAuthn passkeys support sign-in without typing an email or password, with user verification, single-use challenges and clone detection. Password sign-in can require a short-lived TOTP challenge, with encrypted secrets, replay protection and ten one-time recovery codes.

approach.title: An identity other apps can use
approach.body: A headless OpenID Connect provider supports authorization code flow with PKCE, discovery, userinfo and consent for third-party clients, plus token introspection and revocation endpoints. Access and ID tokens use rotating ES256 signing keys published through JWKS, so other services can verify them.

approach.title: Sessions you can actually end
approach.body: Opaque refresh tokens rotate on every use; reuse revokes the session. Every authenticated API request checks that its server-side session is active. Users can list sessions, revoke one, log out everywhere and inspect a paginated login history.

approach.title: The whole account lifecycle
approach.body: Email verification, password reset and confirmed email changes use single-use codes stored as HMACs, with attempt limits and resend cooldowns. Users can edit their profile, export their account data and delete their account after re-authentication.

approach.title: Security at each boundary
approach.body: Argon2id replaces bcrypt, upgrading existing hashes on sign-in. Breached password screening uses k-anonymity, failed sign-ins trigger account lockout, and recovery endpoints avoid revealing whether an account exists. Rate limits can share a Redis store, with Helmet, strict CORS and validated configuration around the API.

approach.title: Delivery and operations built in
approach.body: A PostgreSQL outbox commits email and security notices with the change that caused them, then retries delivery through workers. OpenTelemetry traces and business metrics, redacted structured logs, health checks and OpenAPI docs make the service inspectable. Integration tests use a real database; CI scans code and container images.

highlights: Passwordless WebAuthn passkeys and TOTP with one-time recovery codes
OpenID Connect with PKCE, consent and rotating ES256 keys
Refresh token reuse detection and immediate session revocation in the API
Confirmed email changes, account data export and self-service deletion
Transactional email outbox, security alerts and an account activity log
OpenTelemetry, OpenAPI, database integration tests and container security scans

words.tagline: Sleep logging with weekly analytics: a FastAPI service and a retro-styled Next.js client.
words.summary: A FastAPI and PostgreSQL API that logs sleep sessions with quality ratings and computes statistics, a timeline and weekly summaries with a consistency score, paired with a retro-styled Next.js client that charts them.
words.problem: Logging sleep is easy. Turning the log into something you can act on, like how consistent your week was, takes analysis on the server and an account system that holds up.

approach.body: FastAPI with Tortoise ORM on PostgreSQL, schema migrations with Aerich, and interactive OpenAPI documentation at /docs and /redoc out of the box.

approach.title: Analytics on the server

Weekly consistency score computed server-side

sleep-track.subject: Update the SleepTrack case study for v2

words.tagline: A sleep journal with an analytics engine: an async FastAPI service and a Next.js and daisyUI app.
words.summary: SleepTrack turns logged nights into a nightly score, trends, a chronotype estimate, the habits that help or hurt your sleep and a weekly report. Version 2 is a ground-up rewrite: an async FastAPI service on PostgreSQL and Redis with a background worker, and a Next.js 16 app typed from the API's OpenAPI schema.
words.problem: Logging sleep is the easy part. Making the log useful means knowing which night a session belongs to, which habits change your sleep and how steady your schedule really is, all in your own time zone and behind an account system you can trust with health data.

approach.title: Analytics that respect the clock
approach.body: Bedtimes are averaged as angles, so 23:30 and 00:30 average to midnight instead of noon, and every night belongs to the date it began in the user's time zone. The API computes a weighted score from duration, quality, latency, awakenings and bedtime, plus consistency, sleep debt, streaks, chronotype and social jet lag, cached per user in Redis.

approach.title: Insights in plain language
approach.body: A rule engine behind a pluggable provider compares nights with and without each tag and ranks findings such as caffeine lowering your sleep quality. An ARQ worker emails weekly reports in each user's time zone, sends optional bedtime reminders and clears out demo accounts.

approach.title: Sessions built to be trusted
approach.body: Argon2id passwords, 15-minute access tokens and hashed refresh tokens that rotate on every use: reuse revokes the device, with a short grace window for two tabs refreshing at once. CSRF protection, Redis rate limits, device management, an audit log, email verification and optional Google sign-in with PKCE sit around it.

approach.title: Rules the database enforces
approach.body: PostgreSQL rejects overlapping nights with an exclusion constraint, allows one running timer per user through a partial unique index and searches notes with a trigram index. Every error leaves the API as an RFC 9457 problem document with a stable code.

approach.title: A client typed from the schema
approach.body: The Next.js app generates its types from the OpenAPI schema, keeps the access token in memory and refreshes it single-flight. A same-origin route handler streams /api to the service and forwards the client address, so rate limits see real users. It has two themes, a command menu, a mobile dock and charts with table views.

approach.title: Tested against the real thing
approach.body: Over a thousand backend tests run on real PostgreSQL and Redis, and Playwright drives sign-up with email confirmation, the journal, the timer and settings against the live API in CI. Both repos ship Docker images, a Compose stack and GitHub Actions, and a one-click demo seeds 90 nights.

highlights: Weighted sleep score with circular bedtime statistics, chronotype and tag impact
Rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection and CSRF protection
Overlapping nights rejected by a Postgres exclusion constraint
Weekly email reports and bedtime reminders from a background worker
Client types generated from the API's OpenAPI schema
1,032 backend tests at 98% coverage plus Playwright end-to-end tests in CI
